newsitem.title: USA: Solid demand expected for new U.S. 3-year notes.
newsitem.headline: Solid demand expected for new U.S. 3-year notes.

text.p: Bidding for Tuesday afternoon's three-year note auction should be brisk, but it is unlikely the good demand will spill over to the two other Treasury auctions later this week, market players said.

As part of its quarterly refunding, the Treasury is slated to sell $17.75 billion in three-year notes Tuesday at 1300 EST/1800 GMT, followed by the sale of $12 billion 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10 billion 30-year bonds on Thursday. Results are expected at around 1345 EST/1845 GMT on each day.

"The market has a good bid to it; the dollar had a good bid and commodities prices are tame, so the three-year probably will go pretty well," said Joseph Carson, chief fixed income economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "The trouble comes (at auctions) later in the week when everyone is long and economic news will be pretty strong."
Carson noted that current three-year note levels implies a Federal Reserve on hold for three years.

At around 1045 EST/1545 GMT, the when-issued three-year note was trading at 5.995 percent. Players said they expected the issue to price close to its current level, although some said the market will try to cheapen it up above 6.0 percent ahead of the bidding deadline.

Interest in the new three-year note started early on Tuesday. A number of traders cited a large buyer of the when-issued three-year valued at near $1.0 billion, reportedly bought by a foreign central bank at 5.9975 percent.
And according to GovPX, which tracks volume, the when-issued three-year note was the hottest issue so far today, with $3.2 billion traded by late morning.

"Three year notes are not much of a bellwether and not that popular, so I don't expect them to be a problem," said Kevin Sluder, head trader at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc. "But I also don't expect it will set the tone for the rest of the refunding. People are paying more attention to 10s and bonds. Typically, follow-thorugh (on the three-year) is not that great."

The problem the three-year faces, traders said, is that the market will immediately shift focus to the rest of the refunding and try to cheapen up 10-year notes and 30-year bonds, thereby driving yields up.

"One deciding factor is will there be retail," wondered one trader at a primary dealership. "Retail may not need to buy this week. We're coming off a G7 meeting. There are nerves about the dollar, so the Street may have to underwrite 10s and bonds."

However, he said, there should be strong retail demand for the three-year notes. "They are marginally cheap on the curve and the issue has improved on a spread to twos and fives," the trader said. "The auction should go as well as it usually does."
